deep.reconstruction:
Context (§§110–120 of E260): water runs from an elevated reservoir ('castellum') at height q above a fountain outlet DD, through a pipe of length b and diameter a, with n = b/a. With Euler's friction law the jet height is v = Nq − M. N(n) is a decreasing frictional reduction factor with N(0)=1. M is a loss term that Euler attributes to atmospheric pressure and takes as proportional to it (previous page). Euler's friction depends on pressure, much like Coulomb solid friction, so the ambient pressure enters the loss.

Page 387 draws the practical consequences.

(i) End of §117: q = 130 ft and b = 2500 ft. The tabulated jet heights fall to 4.56 ft at diameter 1/6 ft. For a smaller diameter, about 1/7 ft, Nq < M and no jet emerges.

(ii) §118: water cannot be brought from far away unless the source is very high, because pipes cannot be made very wide. Take one 'milliare', b = 25000 ft, with a = 1/4 ft, so n = 100000. Then N ≈ 1/25 and M ≈ 30, so a jet requires q > M/N = 750 ft. For q = 1000, v = 40 − 30 = 10 ft. For q = 2000, v = 80 − 30 = 50 ft. Each further 1000 ft of head adds only 40 ft of jet.

(iii) §119: without atmospheric pressure M would vanish, v = Nq, and any positive head gives outflow. Euler tabulates n against N:
- N = 1 at n = 0
- 3/4 at 2400; 2/3 at 3500; 1/2 at 6300; 1/3 at 11300; 1/4 at 15700
- 1/5 at 19860; 1/6 at 24000; 1/7 at 28000; 1/8 at 32000; 1/9 at 36000

He reads off the asymptotic rule N ≈ 4000/n for N = 1/ν with ν > 5. Hence on the next page, for long pipes, v ≈ 4000(a/b)q − 30 ft. The atmospheric term then yields the prediction that fountains rise higher when the barometer is low.

The problem served is practical aqueduct and fountain design: pipe routing, choice of diameter, and the feasibility of long conduits.
errors: The physical model is wrong. Euler makes fluid friction proportional to pressure, in analogy with solid friction, so atmospheric pressure produces a loss term M. Modern hydraulics has no such dependence; head loss depends on velocity, length/diameter and roughness, not on ambient pressure. The barometer prediction drawn from it (§120) is therefore spurious.

The asymptotic law v ≈ q/(n/4000) implies, in Darcy–Weisbach terms, a friction factor of about 1/4000. That is roughly 100 times smaller than real pipe friction factors (about 0.02–0.03). The functional dependence on b/a is also not the velocity-squared Darcy form; the large losses come instead from the constant M ≈ 30 ft.
Minor numerical slip in §117 (previous page): 0.3062·130 − 28.660 = 11.15, not 11.19.
The table N ≈ 4000/n is only approximately self-consistent: n = 19860 is listed for N = 1/5 versus 20000 from the rule. Euler restricts the rule to ν > 5, which is fair.
The arithmetic of §118 is internally consistent: 1000/25 − 30 = 10, 2000/25 − 30 = 50, and the increment is 40 ft per 1000 ft of head.

ideas.what: Jet height of a fountain fed through a long pipe declines with length/diameter ratio n = b/a; maximize the diameter and route the pipe straight
ideas.modern_name: Major head loss in pipe flow (Darcy–Weisbach / Chézy-type resistance), hydraulic design of water supply
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Commentarii Acad. Petrop. 6 (1761); discussed by Truesdell in his Opera omnia II.12 introduction (Rational Fluid Mechanics 1687–1765), I believe

ideas.what: Asymptotic rule N ≈ 4000/n, giving jet height ≈ 4000(a/b)q − M for long pipes
ideas.modern_name: Linear head loss proportional to length/diameter (Darcy-type scaling)

ideas.what: Friction proportional to pressure, so the atmosphere reduces fountain height and fountains rise higher at low barometer
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb-type pressure-dependent friction applied to fluids (incorrect for Newtonian flow)

ideas.what: Threshold head q > M/N needed for any outflow; limiting pipe length for given head
ideas.modern_name: Feasibility condition for gravity-fed supply line

missed.claim: Euler gives a concrete, testable but false prediction: fountain height should vary inversely with barometric height. It follows from his pressure-proportional friction. As far as I know this is not usually highlighted as an explicit empirical consequence of the hypothesis that could have refuted it.
missed.quote: sequitur fontes salientes ad eo maiorem altitudinem ascendere debere, quo minus mercurius in Barometro fuerit eleuatus
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Of historical interest only. It illustrates how Euler's friction law could have been tested, and why it was abandoned in favour of velocity-dependent resistance.

deep.surprise_reason: These are numerical applications of a known (and physically incorrect) Euler friction model to fountain design. The calculations are consistent and the ideas are in the published paper. Nothing new to a specialist beyond the curiosity of the barometer prediction.
transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'quam 7/8 ped.' should almost certainly read 'quam 1/7 ped.'. A 7/8 ft threshold contradicts the §117 table, where diameter 1/2 gives v = 52.8 and 1/6 gives v = 4.56, so the threshold lies just below 1/6.
In the §119 table the second fraction (marked [?]) should be 2/3. This fits the monotone sequence and the §117 value N(5000) = 0.5708.
'non vltra altitudinem 10 pedum': the printed '10' looks like 'ao' in the scan but is 10, confirmed by 1000/25 − 30 = 10.
